quote: What is the chief end of man? A. To get rich. In what way? A. Dishonestly if we can; honestly if we must.
source: Mark Twain, The Revised Catechism, the first two questions and answers, New-York Tribune, 27 September 1871, p. 6
note: Corrected to the Tribune’s own wording. The paper prints a catechism: each question stands on its own line and each answer is marked with an A, and there are no dashes. The run together form with dashes comes from quotation books. Page 6 is added. The piece parodies the Westminster Shorter Catechism.

evidence.where: The scanned page itself at the Library of Congress: New-York Tribune, 27 September 1871, page 6, column 1, read as image and as the Library's OCR text. The piece is headed THE REVISED CATECHISM and opens First class in modern Moral Philosophy stand up and recite, then What is the chief end of man ? / A. To get rich. / In what way ? / A. Dishonestly if we can ; honestly if we must. The Center for Mark Twain Studies and twainquotes.com both give the date and the paper, and both print the run together dashed form that the proposal used.
evidence.locator: page 6, column 1, the opening of The Revised Catechism

reason: The line is genuine and the work, date and paper are right, but the proposed wording is a quotation book condensation: it runs four printed lines together, drops the A. that marks each answer, lowercases To get rich and Dishonestly, and inserts two dashes the Tribune never set. The scan shows the catechism form, which is the joke, since What is the chief end of man is the first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism. The paper's title is New-York Tribune with a hyphen, and the page is 6. Twain stands at nothing for the year and is not banned, and the Calendar For Life text, which tacks on but we are all in the Gilded Age now, is not Twain's and is dropped.
